doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Birdland jam sessions and the obnoxious first Embers bassist
summary: She played many welcoming Birdland jam sessions and has no enemies except her first Embers bassist, who kept taking solos and whom she found hard to confront.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Did you subsequently play at Birdland in setting such as that, after that as well?
I played at Birdland a lot, and it was always good. A lot of fun.
I meant like in a jam session type, where . . .
O.k. So it wasn’t just your trio coming into Birdland. It was always one . . .

No, no, I played in jam sessions. I played in a lot of jam sessions. In fact it almost seemed as if . . . sometimes . . . if people would bend over backwards to be especially nice or . . . I don’t know. I really can say I’ve had pretty much good feelings from everybody. I can’t think of anybody that’s an enemy or somebody I have bad feelings about. Except [laughs] a bass player, the first bass player that worked with me in the Embers. I’ve just remembered him. I can’t think what his name was. Bill . . . He was a bass player that would be more or less of a cocktail bass player. I don’t know why I had him. I think I . . . Somebody gave me his name. He was somebody that had a little drinking problem. I would want to end the tune, and he would keep taking another bass solo. Things like that.
That can be a little disconcerting.

He would look at me like, “Man, don’t finish the tune. I’m not . . .” or “Play some more.” He was obnoxious. So I had to . . . It was very hard for me to do that though, to . . . I’m not good at confrontational things.
